**Shift:** At the end of fiscal 2019 (January 31, 2020), Dollar General's primary interest rate exposure was to changes in rates on its variable interest rate debt [1]. By the end of fiscal 2020 (January 29, 2021), it was to changes in rates on its variable rate investment holdings, which were classified as cash and cash equivalents [2].

**Drivers:** The company attributes the increase in cash and cash equivalents primarily to its issuance of $1.5 billion of senior unsecured notes in the first quarter of 2020, to strengthen liquidity amid COVID-19 uncertainty [3]. The debt exposure also fell away. At January 31, 2020 it had commercial paper borrowings of $425.2 million and no Revolving Facility borrowings [4]. At January 29, 2021 it had no commercial paper borrowings and none under the Revolving Facility [5].
